simple: #Bitcoin Internals #1: Bitcoin has rules most holders never read: coins that can never be spent, a bug that once printed 184 billion BTC, a clock allowed to run 2 hours fast. One rule a day, explained simply. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #1: Under the hood, Bitcoin is a set of consensus rules every full node enforces: a 4M weight limit, 2016-block difficulty periods, 100-block coinbase maturity, an 11-block median clock. One rule (or quirk) per day, from the code and the BIPs. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #2: Bitcoin has no accounts and no balances. It tracks unspent coins (UTXOs). Your "balance" is just the sum of the coins your keys can unlock, added up by your wallet. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #2: No account model: the chain state is a set of unspent transaction outputs (UTXOs), each an amount plus a locking script. A transaction consumes whole UTXOs and creates new ones. A wallet's balance is the sum of UTXOs it can spend. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #3: Bitcoin doesn't use decimals inside. Every amount is a whole number of satoshis, and 1 BTC = 100,000,000 sats. You can never send 0.5 sat. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #3: Amounts are 64-bit integers in satoshis: COIN = 100,000,000. No floating point in consensus. MAX_MONEY (21M BTC) is used as a sanity bound: any output or total above it makes the transaction invalid. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #4: The supply cap isn't exactly 21 million. Rewards are rounded down to whole satoshis at each halving, so the real maximum is about 20,999,999.9769 BTC. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #4: Summing the subsidy (50 BTC >> halvings, in integer sats) over 210,000-block eras gives 2,099,999,997,690,000 sats, ≈20,999,999.9769 BTC. Each halving's right shift drops fractions of a satoshi. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #5: Every 210,000 blocks (about 4 years) the new-coin reward per block is cut in half: 50, 25, 12.5, 6.25, and 3.125 BTC since 2024. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #5: GetBlockSubsidy: 50 * COIN >> (height / 210000). Eras so far: 50 → 25 (block 210,000) → 12.5 (420,000) → 6.25 (630,000) → 3.125 BTC (840,000). It is set by block height, not by date. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #6: Bitcoin's halvings so far: Nov 28, 2012; July 9, 2016; May 11, 2020; April 20, 2024. The dates drift because they follow block count, not the calendar. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #6: Halving heights and dates: 210,000 (2012-11-28), 420,000 (2016-07-09), 630,000 (2020-05-11), 840,000 (2024-04-20). Faster-than-10-min blocks pull each one earlier than a strict 4-year schedule. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #7: New bitcoins stop around the year 2140. After 33 halvings, the reward rounds down to zero, and miners live on fees only. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #7: Subsidy = 5,000,000,000 sats >> halvings. After 32 halvings it is 1 sat; at the 33rd (block 6,930,000) it becomes 0. The code also returns 0 if halvings >= 64, to avoid undefined shift behaviour. Expected ≈2140. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #8: The first Bitcoin block (genesis) is dated Jan 3, 2009. It carries a newspaper headline: "The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks". #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #8: Genesis block: timestamp 1231006505 (2009-01-03 18:15:05 UTC), nonce 2083236893, nBits 0x1d00ffff. Its coinbase scriptSig embeds "The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks". #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #9: The 50 BTC reward of the very first block can never be spent. Not because of a lock: the code simply never added that coin to its list of spendable coins. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #9: The genesis block is hardcoded and never connected through normal validation, so its coinbase output never entered the UTXO set. Any transaction trying to spend it fails as spending a missing input. Changing that would need a hard fork. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #10: The first Bitcoin transfer between two people was in block 170, on Jan 12, 2009: Satoshi Nakamoto sent 10 BTC to Hal Finney. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #10: Block 170 (2009-01-12) holds the first non-coinbase transaction: 10 BTC from Satoshi to Hal Finney, spending the coinbase of block 9. Before it, every transaction was a block reward. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #11: A block header is tiny: just 80 bytes. That's all a miner hashes over and over, trillions of times, looking for a winning number. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #11: Header = 80 bytes: version (4), previous block hash (32), merkle root (32), time (4), nBits target (4), nonce (4). Proof of work is SHA-256d of these 80 bytes; transactions are committed only via the merkle root. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #12: Mining means hashing a block header until the result is a number below a target. A lower target means more tries are needed. That's all "difficulty" is. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #12: Proof of work: SHA256(SHA256(header)), read as a 256-bit little-endian number, must be <= the target encoded in nBits (compact float: 1 byte exponent, 3 bytes mantissa). Difficulty = difficulty-1 target / current target. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #13: The block's "nonce" counter only has about 4.3 billion values. Modern miners run through that in a blink, so they also change other parts of the block to keep searching. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #13: The header nonce is 32 bits (≈4.29 billion values). Miners also vary an extraNonce in the coinbase (which changes the merkle root), the timestamp, and some version bits (version rolling, BIP320) to get fresh search space. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #14: Bitcoin aims for one block every 10 minutes. Every 2016 blocks (about 2 weeks) every node recomputes the difficulty to stay on that pace. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #14: nPowTargetSpacing = 600 s, nPowTargetTimespan = 14 days, so the retarget interval is 1,209,600 / 600 = 2016 blocks. Each node computes the new target itself; no one announces it. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #15: Difficulty can't jump wildly: one adjustment can make mining at most 4x harder or 4x easier, however fast or slow the last 2 weeks were. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #15: Retarget clamps the measured timespan to [timespan/4, timespan*4], so one adjustment moves the target by at most a factor of 4 either way. The target is also capped at powLimit (difficulty 1). #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #16: An old quirk: difficulty is meant to measure 2016 block gaps but measures only 2015. That small slip opens the "time warp" attack, where miners fake timestamps to lower difficulty. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #16: Retarget uses the time from the first to the last block of the period: 2015 intervals, not 2016. Periods don't overlap, so a majority of hashrate can backdate timestamps and drive difficulty down over time: the "time warp" attack. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #17: The time warp bug has been fixed on Bitcoin's newest test network (testnet4): the first block of a difficulty period can't be backdated much. Mainnet still has the old rule. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #17: BIP94 (testnet4, shipped in Bitcoin Core 28.0): the first block of a retarget period may not be more than 600 s earlier than the previous block (MAX_TIMEWARP). A mainnet fix is specified in BIP54 (Consensus Cleanup), not activated. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #18: Block timestamps don't have to be exact. A block is valid if its time is later than the middle value of the previous 11 blocks, and not more than 2 hours ahead of your clock. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #18: Timestamp rules: nTime > median time past (MTP) of the last 11 blocks (consensus), and nTime <= node's adjusted time + 2 h (MAX_FUTURE_BLOCK_TIME, local check). So block times can go backwards. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #19: Bitcoin has a far-future date problem: block time is stored in 32 bits, which runs out in the year 2106. Fixing it will need a change to the rules. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #19: Header nTime is a uint32 of Unix seconds, so it overflows after 4,294,967,295 = 2106-02-07 06:28:15 UTC. Any fix changes how headers are validated, so it needs a consensus change well before then. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #20: Miners can't spend new block rewards right away. They must wait 100 blocks (about 17 hours), in case their block gets replaced by another. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #20: COINBASE_MATURITY = 100: a coinbase output can be spent only 100 or more blocks after the block that created it. A reorg would erase the coinbase, so this stops it from spreading into transactions that would then become invalid. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #21: A miner may claim less than the full reward, never more. Whatever they don't claim is lost forever. It has happened, through bugs and mistakes. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #21: Consensus checks coinbase output total <= subsidy + fees, not ==. Any shortfall is never created and is permanently out of supply. A few early and buggy blocks underclaimed, which is part of why the real supply ends below the cap. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #22: In 2010, someone made a transaction worth about 184 billion BTC. A number in the code overflowed. Within about 5 hours a fixed version was out, and the bad block was dropped. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #22: Value overflow incident, Aug 15, 2010, block 74638: two outputs of ≈92.2 billion BTC each overflowed the 64-bit sum check. The fix rejected such outputs; once upgraded miners overtook it, the chain without the bad tx won. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #23: Two pairs of Bitcoin blocks have reward transactions with the exact same ID. Each pair counts only once: two 50 BTC rewards vanished. A rule (BIP30) now forbids this. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #23: Coinbases in blocks 91,812/91,842 and 91,722/91,880 share txids; the later one overwrote the earlier in the UTXO set (50 BTC lost per pair). BIP30 bans a txid matching an unspent one; 91,842 and 91,880 are hardcoded exceptions. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #24: Since 2013, each block must write its own block number inside its reward transaction. That makes every reward transaction unique. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #24: BIP34 (enforced from block 227,931): the coinbase scriptSig must start with the block height. Different heights give different coinbase txids, so BIP30-style duplicates can't occur in normal operation. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #25: Sept 2018: a bug in Bitcoin Core could have let a miner create coins from nothing by spending the same coin twice in one transaction. It was patched quietly first, then disclosed. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #25: CVE-2018-17144: Core 0.14 to 0.16.2 skipped a duplicate-input check (a crash bug); from 0.15 it could also inflate supply. Fixed in 0.16.3 (Sept 18, 2018), full disclosure Sept 20. No exploitation was known. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #26: March 2013: Bitcoin split into two chains for a few hours because two versions of the software disagreed on one big block. Miners chose to roll back to the old version's chain. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #26: BIP50: a block valid under 0.8 (LevelDB) needed more database locks than pre-0.8 (Berkeley DB) allowed, so the network split. Pools downgraded to 0.7 so its chain won, and 0.8 nodes reorganized onto it. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #27: A block doesn't list its transactions in the header. It stores one fingerprint (the merkle root) that sums up all of them. Change one transaction and it changes. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #27: The merkle root is a binary tree of SHA-256d txids. A light client checks a tx is in a block with log2(n) hashes: ≈12 hashes for a 4,000-tx block, instead of downloading the whole block. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #28: Bitcoin's transaction tree has a quirk: copying the last transaction can give the same fingerprint. In 2012 that could trick nodes into rejecting good blocks. It's handled now. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #28: CVE-2012-2459: with an odd count, the last merkle node is paired with itself, so duplicating the last txs keeps the same root. Nodes could cache that block hash as invalid and reject the real block. Now this mutation is detected. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #29: There is no "fee" field in a Bitcoin transaction. The fee is whatever you don't send: coins going in minus coins going out. The miner keeps the difference. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #29: fee = sum(inputs) - sum(outputs). It is implicit, never written in the tx. Consensus only requires inputs >= outputs; the miner claims all fees in the block's coinbase. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #30: You can't spend part of a coin. To pay 0.3 BTC from a 1 BTC coin, you spend all of it: 0.3 to the payee and the rest back to yourself as "change". #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #30: A UTXO is spent whole. Wallets add a change output back to a new address of their own. Forget the change output and the whole remainder becomes miner fee. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #31: A transaction can be locked until a future date or block. The same number means a block height if it's small, or a date if it's big. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #31: nLockTime < 500,000,000 is a block height; >= 500,000,000 is a Unix timestamp (Nov 5, 1985). Since BIP113, time locks compare against median time past, not the block's own timestamp. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #32: Coins can be locked inside a script so they can't move before a set date. That rule (2015) made things like time-locked savings and payment channels possible. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #32: BIP65 OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY, enforced from block 388,381: the script fails unless the spending tx's nLockTime is past the value in the script. It reused the OP_NOP2 opcode, so it was a soft fork. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #33: Bitcoin also has relative time locks: "this coin can move only 1,000 blocks after it was received". That's what makes Lightning's safety windows work. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #33: BIP68/112/113 (CSV), active at block 419,328: nSequence encodes a relative lock in blocks or 512-s units, OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY enforces it in script, and BIP113 uses median time past for time locks. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #34: Bitcoin has its own small programming language, Script. It has no loops on purpose, so every script finishes and can't hang the network. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #34: Script is a stack-based, Forth-like language with no loops or jumps, so execution length is bounded by script size. A spend is valid if scriptSig/witness + scriptPubKey run without error and leave a true value on top. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #35: In 2010 Satoshi switched off several Script commands, including OP_CAT, after bugs were found. Proposals to bring OP_CAT back are still debated today. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #35: In 2010 OP_CAT, OP_SUBSTR, OP_MUL, OP_LSHIFT and others were disabled: any script containing them fails, even in an unexecuted branch. Re-enabling OP_CAT in tapscript is proposed in BIP347, not active. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #36: Bitcoin scripts have hard limits so no transaction can overload a node: size, number of steps and size of each piece of data are all capped. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #36: Legacy/SegWit v0 script limits: 10,000 bytes per script, 201 non-push opcodes, 520 bytes per stack element, 1,000 stack items, 20 keys per OP_CHECKMULTISIG. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #37: A bug from 2009 still lives in Bitcoin: multisig takes one more item than it needs. Every multisig spend carries an extra useless zero because of it. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #37: OP_CHECKMULTISIG pops one extra stack element. It can't be removed without a hard fork, so spenders push a dummy OP_0. BIP147 (NULLDUMMY, with SegWit) requires that dummy to be empty, closing a malleability vector. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #38: Some outputs are provably unspendable: those starting with OP_RETURN. They're used to write small data on chain, and nodes can forget them because nobody can ever spend them. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #38: A scriptPubKey starting with OP_RETURN fails whenever executed, so the output can never be spent. Nodes don't add these outputs to the UTXO set, keeping it smaller. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #39: Addresses starting with "3" came in 2012. They let you send to a complex wallet (like 2-of-3 multisig) while the sender only sees a short address. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #39: BIP16 P2SH, enforced from April 1, 2012 (timestamp 1333238400): the output commits to HASH160 of a redeem script; the spender reveals the script and its inputs. Version byte 0x05 gives "3" addresses. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #40: Bitcoin addresses tell you their type by their start: 1 = original, 3 = script, bc1q = SegWit, bc1p = Taproot. They all send the same bitcoin. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #40: Mainnet address prefixes: "1" P2PKH (Base58Check, 0x00), "3" P2SH (0x05), "bc1q" witness v0 (bech32, BIP173), "bc1p" witness v1 Taproot (bech32m, BIP350). Addresses aren't on chain; scripts are. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #41: Old Bitcoin addresses never contain 0, O, I or l. Satoshi left them out so nobody mixes them up when copying an address by hand. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #41: Base58 alphabet: 0-9, A-Z, a-z minus 0, O, I and l. Base58Check appends a 4-byte checksum (first bytes of SHA-256d), so most typos are caught before sending. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #42: Taproot addresses (bc1p) use a slightly different checksum than SegWit ones (bc1q). The first format had a small weakness, so it was patched for new address types. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #42: Bech32 (BIP173) has a flaw: if an address ends in "p", inserting or deleting "q" chars just before it can go undetected. BIP350 bech32m changes the checksum constant and is used for witness v1+ (Taproot). #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #43: An old-style address is not your public key: it's a 20-byte fingerprint of it. Your public key only appears on chain when you spend. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #43: P2PKH and P2WPKH commit to HASH160(pubkey) = RIPEMD-160(SHA-256(pubkey)), 20 bytes. The full key is revealed in the spending input. Taproot outputs, by contrast, hold a 32-byte key directly. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #44: Bitcoin's keys use an elliptic curve called secp256k1, rare when Satoshi chose it. Your private key is just a 256-bit number. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #44: Keys are on secp256k1 (y² = x³ + 7 over a 256-bit prime field). A private key is an integer below the group order n ≈ 1.158×10^77; the public key is that integer times the generator point G. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #45: The 1 MB block size limit wasn't in the first version. Satoshi added it in 2010, without much explanation. It became the center of years of debate. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #45: MAX_BLOCK_SIZE = 1,000,000 bytes was added to the code by Satoshi in 2010. Raising it would be a hard fork; SegWit replaced it in 2017 with a 4M weight limit, a soft fork that old nodes still accept. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #46: SegWit went live on Aug 24, 2017. It moved signatures to a separate part of the transaction, which fixed an old bug and made room for more transactions. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #46: SegWit (BIP141/143/144) activated at block 481,824 on 2017-08-24. Witness data is kept outside the legacy tx serialization and committed in the coinbase via an OP_RETURN witness commitment. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #47: Bitcoin blocks aren't limited to 1 MB anymore. Since SegWit, the limit is in "weight": signature data counts 4x less than the rest. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #47: Block weight = 3 x base size + total size, limit 4,000,000 WU (MAX_BLOCK_WEIGHT). A non-witness byte = 4 WU, a witness byte = 1 WU. Fees are quoted in vbytes = weight / 4. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #48: Before SegWit, anyone could slightly change a transaction's ID before it was confirmed, without stealing anything. That broke apps that tracked payments by ID. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #48: Txid malleability: a third party could re-encode signatures (e.g. flip ECDSA s to n-s) and change the txid. SegWit txids exclude witness data, which made unconfirmed chains of txs (needed by Lightning) safe. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #49: The biggest Bitcoin block so far was about 3.96 MB, mined in Feb 2023. Most of it was one picture, an NFT-style inscription. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #49: Block 774,628 (Feb 1, 2023), mined by Luxor, ≈3.96 MB, nearly all a single Taproot witness inscription (a "Taproot Wizard" image). Large witness data is cheap in weight, so a block can reach about 4 MB. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #50: Inscriptions ("Bitcoin NFTs") store data in the signature part of a transaction, which is cheaper in weight. It's a use the protocol allows, not a special feature. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #50: Ordinals inscriptions put data in a Taproot script-path witness inside an unexecuted OP_FALSE OP_IF ... OP_ENDIF envelope. Tapscript has no 10,000-byte script limit, so data is bounded only by block weight. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #51: In 2015 Bitcoin forced all signatures into one strict format. Some old software accepted odd variants, which was risky since not all versions read them the same way. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #51: BIP66 strict DER signatures, enforced from block 363,725: ECDSA signatures must use strict DER encoding. Before that, validity depended on OpenSSL's lax parsing, which could differ across platforms. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #52: Taproot, Bitcoin's last big upgrade, went live on Nov 14, 2021. It brought new signatures and better privacy for complex wallets. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #52: Taproot (BIP340 Schnorr, BIP341 Taproot, BIP342 Tapscript) activated at block 709,632 on 2021-11-14, after Speedy Trial signaling with a 90% threshold (1,815 of 2,016 blocks). #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #53: Taproot added Schnorr signatures: shorter than the old kind, and several signers can combine their keys into one signature that looks like a single person's. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #53: BIP340 Schnorr signatures are a fixed 64 bytes (ECDSA DER: up to 72) with 32-byte x-only public keys. Linearity allows key aggregation (e.g. MuSig2, BIP327), so an n-of-n multisig looks like a single-key spend. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #54: With Taproot, a coin can have many hidden spending rules. When you spend it, you reveal only the rule you used. The others stay private forever. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #54: BIP341: the output key commits to an internal key plus a merkle tree of scripts (MAST). Key-path spends reveal nothing about scripts; script-path spends reveal one leaf plus a merkle proof. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #55: Taproot also left room for future upgrades: many unused commands are reserved so later soft forks can give them a meaning safely. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #55: BIP342 tapscript: opcodes 80, 98, 126-129, 131-134, 137-138, 141-142, 149-153, 187-254 become OP_SUCCESSx; any script containing one is valid until a soft fork defines it. Leaf versions add another upgrade path. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #56: Taproot scripts dropped some old limits, like the 201-step cap. A spend's "signature budget" now grows with the size of the data you pay for. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #56: BIP342: in tapscript the 10,000-byte script limit and 201 non-push opcode limit don't apply. Sigops get a per-input budget of 50 + witness size in bytes, and each signature check costs 50. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #57: Old Bitcoin software still follows today's chain after an upgrade. That's a soft fork: new rules only make things stricter, so old nodes see new blocks as valid. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #57: Soft fork: tightens the rules, so blocks valid under new rules are still valid to old nodes (P2SH, CLTV, CSV, SegWit, Taproot). Hard fork: loosens them, so non-upgraded nodes reject the new blocks and the chain splits. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #58: How does Bitcoin decide to upgrade? For years miners signaled readiness inside blocks; an upgrade locked in when 95% of blocks in a 2-week period signaled. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #58: BIP9 versionbits: miners set a bit in the header version; a deployment locks in when 1,916 of 2,016 blocks (95%) in one retarget period signal, then activates one period later. Used for CSV and SegWit. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #59: Bitcoin's longest chain is not the one with the most blocks. It's the one with the most total work behind it. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #59: Nodes follow the valid chain with the most cumulative proof of work (sum of 2^256 / (target+1) per block), not the highest block count. A long chain of low-difficulty blocks loses to a shorter but harder one. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #60: Why wait several confirmations? The whitepaper's math: an attacker with 10% of mining power has under a 0.1% chance to undo a payment 5 blocks deep. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #60: Whitepaper, section 11: with q = 0.1 attacker hashrate, P < 0.001 at z = 5 blocks (0.0009137). At q = 0.3 it takes z = 24. "6 confirmations" is a convention, not a protocol rule. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #61: There's no single global queue of pending transactions. Each node keeps its own "mempool" (300 MB by default), so two nodes can see different pending lists. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #61: The mempool is local policy, not consensus. Bitcoin Core default -maxmempool = 300 MB; when full it evicts the lowest-feerate txs and raises its min feerate. Miners can include any valid tx, mempool or not. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #62: A stuck transaction can be replaced by a new version paying a higher fee. Since Bitcoin Core 28.0 (2024), nodes accept such replacements by default. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #62: Replace-by-fee: BIP125 made it opt-in via nSequence signaling. Bitcoin Core 28.0 made -mempoolfullrbf default to true, so a higher-fee replacement is relayed whatever the signal. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #63: Network rules vs node habits: the 4M weight limit is consensus, but nodes by default refuse to relay any single transaction above a tenth of that. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #63: Policy, not consensus: MAX_STANDARD_TX_WEIGHT = 400,000 WU, so non-standard txs aren't relayed by default Bitcoin Core nodes. A miner can still include up to the 4,000,000 WU block limit. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #64: "Dust" is an output so small it would cost more in fees to spend than it's worth. Nodes refuse to relay most of them by default. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #64: Dust policy: an output is dust if spending it costs more than its value at 3 sat/vB (DUST_RELAY_TX_FEE = 3000 sat/kvB). That gives 546 sats for P2PKH and 294 for P2WPKH. Policy only, not consensus. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #65: Since Bitcoin Core 30.0 (Oct 2025), nodes by default relay transactions paying as little as 0.1 sat per vbyte, 10x lower than before. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #65: Bitcoin Core 30.0 lowered the -minrelaytxfee and -incrementalrelayfee defaults from 1 to 0.1 sat/vB (100 sat/kvB). Wallet fee estimates weren't changed; low-fee txs only propagate as nodes upgrade. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #66: Bitcoin nodes talk on port 8333, and every network message starts with the same 4 magic bytes, so nodes can tell mainnet from testnet traffic. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #66: Mainnet P2P: default port 8333, message start (magic) bytes 0xF9 0xBE 0xB4 0xD9. Each message has a 24-byte header: magic, 12-byte command, payload length, 4-byte checksum. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #67: New blocks spread fast because nodes don't resend transactions they already have. They send a short summary, and peers rebuild the block from their mempool. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #67: BIP152 compact blocks: a node sends the header plus 6-byte short tx IDs (SipHash) and a few prefilled txs; the peer fills the rest from its mempool and only asks for what's missing. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #68: You can run a full node without storing the whole blockchain. A pruned node checks everything, then deletes old blocks, keeping as little as about 550 MB. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #68: -prune: the node fully validates every block, then deletes old block and undo files. Minimum target is 550 MiB (MIN_DISK_SPACE_FOR_BLOCK_FILES). It keeps the UTXO set but can't serve old blocks to peers. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #69: Your 12 or 24 recovery words aren't stored on the blockchain. They're a human-friendly encoding of one big random number your wallet derives all keys from. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #69: BIP39: entropy (128-256 bits) plus a checksum split into 11-bit words from a 2048-word list gives 12-24 words, stretched by PBKDF2 into a seed. BIP32 derives a key tree from it. None of this is consensus. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #70: When you sign a transaction, you choose what your signature covers. Usually all of it, but some flags let others add inputs or outputs later. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #70: Sighash flags: ALL, NONE, SINGLE, each optionally combined with ANYONECANPAY. Taproot adds SIGHASH_DEFAULT (0x00, same as ALL with no extra byte), so its signatures stay 64 bytes. #BTC #Crypto

simple: #Bitcoin Internals #71: That's the series: no accounts, a cap of about 20,999,999.9769 BTC, 100-block maturity, a 2-hour clock window, the 2010 overflow bug, SegWit, Taproot. The rules live in the code. Follow for more. #BTC #Crypto
tech: #Bitcoin Internals #71: Recap: UTXOs, integer sats, 2016-block retargets clamped at 4x, MTP-11 timestamps, BIP30/34 duplicate fixes, 4M weight, Schnorr and MAST, policy vs consensus. Bitcoin is its rules, and anyone can check them. Follow for more. #BTC #Crypto
